stages.name: Source
stages.description: Where data originates: the operational systems, applications and feeds that produce it.
stages.rationale: The systems data comes from usually sit outside the stack, so having no source tool is normal and never a gap.

stages.name: Ingest
stages.description: Moving data from sources into the platform.
stages.rationale: Data has to arrive somewhere, though a stack that works inside its own platform can do without.

stages.name: Store
stages.description: Where data rests and how it is laid out for analytical use.
stages.rationale: Nothing works without somewhere to keep the data.

stages.name: Transform
stages.description: Reshaping raw data into modelled, trustworthy datasets.
stages.rationale: Raw data is rarely fit to use, though simple reporting can skip it.

stages.name: Orchestrate
stages.description: Deciding when work runs, in what order, and how changes are shipped.
stages.rationale: Work can be started by hand or by scripts, which is painful but not fatal.

stages.name: Serve
stages.description: Getting data to the people, applications and models that use it.
stages.rationale: Data nobody can reach has no value.

bands.name: Govern
bands.description: Knowing what data exists and controlling who can do what with it.

bands.name: Quality
bands.description: Detecting and preventing incorrect, late or malformed data.

bands.name: Observe
bands.description: Seeing what the system is doing, where data came from, and what it costs.

bands.name: Platform
bands.description: The infrastructure, environments and developer workflow the work happens in.

source.oltp.name: Transactional database
source.oltp.description: Can act as the operational system of record behind an application. Scored when the tool is itself such an origin, not when it merely connects to one.

source.saas-api.name: SaaS application data
source.saas-api.description: Holds business data in a hosted application and exposes it through an API or export.

source.file-drop.name: File drop
source.file-drop.description: Receives or exposes files (CSV, JSON, Parquet, partner extracts) by upload, SFTP or shared storage.

source.event-stream.name: Event stream
source.event-stream.description: Emits or hosts a continuous feed of application, device or clickstream events.

ingest.batch-extract.name: Batch extract
ingest.batch-extract.description: Scheduled or on-demand bulk extraction from source systems into the platform.

ingest.cdc.name: Change data capture
ingest.cdc.description: Log-based or incremental capture of row-level changes from databases.

ingest.stream-ingest.name: Stream ingest
ingest.stream-ingest.description: Continuous ingestion of event streams with defined delivery semantics.

ingest.reverse-etl.name: Reverse ETL
ingest.reverse-etl.description: Pushing modelled data back into operational and SaaS systems.

store.object-store.name: Object store
store.object-store.description: Durable, cheap, schema-less storage for files and blobs.

store.table-format.name: Table format
store.table-format.description: Transactional table layer over files (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi style): ACID, schema evolution, time travel.

store.warehouse.name: Warehouse
store.warehouse.description: Managed analytical store with SQL access, separating modelled data from raw files.

store.olap-serving.name: OLAP serving
store.olap-serving.description: Low-latency analytical store built to answer many concurrent aggregate queries.

transform.sql-transform.name: SQL transformation
transform.sql-transform.description: Modelling and reshaping data by authoring SQL.

transform.code-transform.name: Code transformation
transform.code-transform.description: Modelling and reshaping data in a general-purpose language (Python, Scala, Spark).

transform.stream-processing.name: Stream processing
transform.stream-processing.description: Stateful transformation of events as they arrive: windows, joins, aggregations.

transform.feature-eng.name: Feature engineering
transform.feature-eng.description: Producing, storing and reusing model features, including point-in-time correctness.

orchestrate.scheduling.name: Scheduling
orchestrate.scheduling.description: Running work on a time-based schedule.

orchestrate.dependency-dag.name: Dependency DAG
orchestrate.dependency-dag.description: Expressing and executing task dependencies, retries and backfills.

orchestrate.event-triggers.name: Event triggers
orchestrate.event-triggers.description: Starting work in response to data arrival or external events rather than the clock.

orchestrate.ci-cd.name: CI/CD
orchestrate.ci-cd.description: Testing and promoting pipeline code and definitions across environments.

serve.query-engine.name: Query engine
serve.query-engine.description: Interactive SQL access for analysts, tools and applications.

serve.semantic-layer.name: Semantic layer
serve.semantic-layer.description: Governed, reusable metric and dimension definitions that sit between data and consumers.

serve.bi-viz.name: BI and visualisation
serve.bi-viz.description: Dashboards, reports and exploratory analysis for business users.

serve.data-apps.name: Data apps
serve.data-apps.description: Building interactive applications on top of data.

serve.ml-serving.name: ML serving
serve.ml-serving.description: Deploying trained models and exposing predictions to consumers.

govern.catalog.name: Catalog
govern.catalog.description: Inventory of data assets with ownership, descriptions and search.

govern.access-control.name: Access control
govern.access-control.description: Deciding who can read or change which data.

govern.masking.name: Masking
govern.masking.description: Obscuring or tokenising sensitive values while keeping data usable.

govern.policy.name: Policy
govern.policy.description: Defining and enforcing data-handling rules such as retention, residency and classification.

quality.tests.name: Data tests
quality.tests.description: Assertions on data that pass or fail: uniqueness, nulls, referential integrity, custom rules.

quality.contracts.name: Data contracts
quality.contracts.description: Agreed, enforceable schema and semantics at a producer-consumer boundary.

quality.anomaly-detection.name: Anomaly detection
quality.anomaly-detection.description: Detecting unexpected change in volume, freshness, distribution or schema without hand-written rules.

observe.monitoring.name: Monitoring
observe.monitoring.description: Health, freshness and failure visibility, with alerting.

observe.lineage.name: Lineage
observe.lineage.description: Tracing where data came from and what depends on it.

observe.cost-visibility.name: Cost visibility
observe.cost-visibility.description: Attributing spend to workloads, teams and datasets.

platform.infra.name: Infrastructure
platform.infra.description: Provisioning and running the compute and storage underneath, including infrastructure as code.

platform.environments.name: Environments
platform.environments.description: Separate dev, test and production spaces with safe promotion between them.

platform.dev-experience.name: Developer experience
platform.dev-experience.description: Tooling that makes authoring, running and debugging work productive: editors, IDEs, local runs, CLIs.

criticality.scale: 0 = not applicable, never surfaces as a gap. 1 = nice to have. 2 = useful. 3 = expected in a mature stack. 4 = important. 5 = a gap here undermines the stack.

govern.rationale: Peaks where data rests and where it is exposed. Little is controllable at origin, and orchestration moves no data values.

quality.rationale: Cheapest to catch early. Peaks at ingest and transform where defects enter or are introduced, and tapers toward the edges.

observe.rationale: Peaks where jobs run and fail, and where spend accrues.

platform.rationale: Environments and workflow matter most where code is written and deployed.

overrides.rationale: Orchestrators rarely own the spend. Cost shows up in the engine that runs the work.
Storage and warehouse compute are usually the dominant cost lines.
Contracts exist to fix the one thing quality checks can't: defects that originate upstream.
Orchestration passes no data values through, so there is nothing to mask.
Lineage traces data, and data moves through the engines that do the work, not the scheduler. Monitoring is what matters at this stage.
